Devlog: October 2026

51 updates to Tailwinds in October 2026, newest first. The devlog index lists every month.

October 31, 2026

City loyalty: frequent flyers you have to win (new games)

The loyalty program has been rebuilt for new games. The weekly budget is gone; members are now something you win from the other airlines, city by city.

  • Frequent flyers live in cities. Every city has its own frequent flyers, and every airline flying there competes for them. The more you fly from a city and the better your program, the more of them carry your card. Most people carry no card at all unless a program is worth it.
  • The AI airlines run programs too. Full-service carriers are strongest at their own hubs, and budget carriers barely bother. You won’t take a fortress hub from its owner, but you can own the cities around it.
  • What makes a program worth joining is mostly what your airline already is: how generous it is, a lounge in that city your members can use, a free checked bag, premium cabins, an alliance, how many places you fly from the city, travel partners working there, and being on time.
  • Loyalty only decides which airline people fly. It never adds travellers to a market. On a route nobody else flies it changes nothing; where you compete, your members choose you and shrug off a cheaper fare.
  • One setting: generosity, the share of the fare members earn back (3–12%). Raising it is free. Cutting it is a devaluation: members walk out, your cities shop around for 8 weeks, and your reputation takes a hit.
  • Status match. Now and then an AI airline devalues its program. You then have 3 weeks to honour its members’ status in the cities you both fly and take half of the ones walking out.
  • The status year. Every December elites requalify against the flying you kept up in their city. Cut a city’s routes and its elites leave with them. Elites also leave unreliable airlines first.
  • See it on the map. Turn on the Loyalty layer on the Network map to see who holds each city’s frequent flyers. The Loyalty page lists every city, your share against your biggest rival, and what your program is worth there.

Games started before today keep the budget-and-tier program.

October 30, 2026

Brand marketing on the Dashboard

The Dashboard has a new Brand Marketing / wk tile showing what your brand marketing costs this week. If it’s held at a % of revenue, the tile shows that share and last week’s spend next to it, so you can see it growing with the airline. On a fixed budget, it shows what share of your revenue that budget comes to. Targeted airport campaigns are listed separately. Click the tile to go straight to the marketing settings.

Suggested by VodkaOnFire on Discord.

October 30, 2026

Travel partnerships: cruise lines, tour operators, hotels and ride share

New games can now sign travel partners under Company → Partnerships. Each one brings extra travellers to the airports it works in, and wants something back.

  • Leisure or business. Cruise lines and tour operators bring more leisure travellers; hotel chains and ride share bring more business travellers, on routes to their airports. Cruise lines only sail in their season, such as the Caribbean from November to April and Alaska from May to September.
  • Every partner has targets. Passengers delivered into its airports, how many of them you serve, departures, on-time rate, route quality, a business cabin. The page shows last week’s figures against every target before you sign, and roughly how happy each partner would be with you.
  • Keep them happy. Meet the brief and a partner settles around 80 happiness; beat it to delight them. Unhappy partners promote you less and cost you reputation. Below 15 for four weeks they walk out, and won’t work with you again for five years.
  • Two-year deals. Delighted partners renew at 40% off; frustrated ones charge more and raise their targets. Auto-renew is on unless you turn it off.

Partnerships come with new games only; existing saves are unchanged. See Demand & Quality for how leisure and business travellers choose an airline.

October 30, 2026

A better logo maker, rival colours, and your own airline code

Your airline’s look got a proper overhaul, both when you start a game and under Edit Branding:

  • Pick your airline code. Choose a two-character code, the way Qantas is QF and United is UA. It starts your flight numbers on the departure board. Leave it blank and the game suggests one from your airline’s name.
  • A second colour. Every logo used to sit on the same dark tile. Now you choose the tile colour too, from deep navy and burgundy to the full palette, or pick any colour you like for the logo and the tile. If the two are too close to read, the game warns you. Uploaded logos with a transparent background sit on your tile colour.
  • Cleaner tails. On your aircraft the logo is now painted straight onto the tail and fuselage instead of on a dark square. If your logo colour would disappear into the paint, the mark switches to white (or dark on pale paint), so a red mark on a red tail becomes a white one. Prefer the old look? Tick Logo on its tile on the Livery tab.
  • Rivals have their own colours. Rival airlines all used to show in the same blue, and a few shared identical logos. Each rival now has its own colour to suit its style (bright for budget carriers, gold and violet for premium ones), and no two airlines, you included, share the same logo in the same colour. Rival codes are now the same at every airport, and they show on each rival’s card on the Competition page.
  • See it at every size. The preview now shows your logo and code the way they appear on the departure board as well as full size.

October 30, 2026

Clear all pop-ups, and choose which ones you see

Later in a game the weekly pop-ups pile up: breakdowns, deliveries, rivals entering your routes. Thanks to Xen and VodkaOnFire on Discord for asking for a way to deal with them:

  • Clear all. When two or more pop-ups are on screen, a small bar above them shows how many there are and a Clear all button. You can also press Delete (or Backspace, the Mac delete key) to clear them all. Nothing happens while you’re typing in a box.
  • Choose which pop-ups show. The new 🔔 Pop-up alerts button, in the top bar (in the ⋯ menu on phones) or under ⚙ Settings in the map view, lets you turn weekly pop-ups off altogether or by kind: breakdowns & maintenance, fleet & leases, rivals, cash & loans, bases & gates & crew, and world events. Your choice is remembered on this device.
  • Nothing is lost. The same panel lists the pop-ups youThe same panel lists the week’s recent pop-ups, including the ones you’ve hidden.rsquo;ve had since you opened the game, hidden ones included. Pop-ups about something you just did, like “Not enough cash”, always show, and so does a warning that your game isn’t saving.

October 30, 2026

Real-world demand goes global (new games)

Yesterday’s demand overhaul checked the game against real traffic in the US and Australia. New games now get the same treatment almost everywhere else. We compared passenger demand with official route statistics from the EU, the UK, Switzerland, Norway, Turkey, Brazil, Mexico, India and Japan, and every international route to and from the US and Australia:

  • Holiday routes are as big as they really are. Palma, the Canaries, the Greek islands, Faro, Dalaman, Los Cabos and Goa now draw two to five times the passengers they did. London–Palma goes from about 5,800 to 13,100 a week, close to the real 14,100. Some country pairs pull far harder than distance and size suggest: the UK and the Caribbean, Germany and Egypt, Spain and the Dominican Republic.
  • Each country flies the amount it really does. Italy, Spain, Portugal and the UK fly more at home. India, Brazil, Japan and Mexico flew far too much and come down: Delhi–Mumbai and Tokyo–Sapporo are now close to their real figures.
  • Every airport is matched to its real traffic. Busy airports with bigger catchments than their city gain, quiet ones lose, and airports without their own data take their region’s figure.
  • Seasons for about 1,000 airports. Seasons now come from real monthly traffic. Greek and Turkish resorts are nearly empty in winter, the Canaries and Lapland peak in winter, Alpine ski airports from December to March, and transatlantic and transpacific routes in summer. Business hubs run flatter than the holiday routes they serve.
  • Small US airports keep their international travellers. Yesterday’s update cut every route out of a small US airport, international ones included. Those cuts now apply only to US domestic routes, and international demand from US airports follows its own real data.

As before, we stopped about two-thirds of the way to the real numbers, so regional flying stays playable. Overall there is about 9% less demand than in yesterday’s model. Games already running keep the demand they started with. More on how demand works in the route economics guide.

October 30, 2026

Crew replacements now stay ahead of leavers while you grow

With Replace leavers automatically on, a growing airline could still find itself a few crew short for a week or two, usually just after new aircraft arrived. Thanks to the player on Discord who reported it. Three fixes:

  • Crew training for new aircraft are no longer mistaken for spare staff. While you had pilots in training for an aircraft on order, the automatic replacements counted them as extra people and stopped replacing leavers. A few weeks after the aircraft landed, the gap showed up. Replacements now keep going while your new crews train.
  • Replacements skip the recruiting queue. A big hire for new aircraft can take several weeks to recruit, and replacements used to wait behind it. They now start training straight away, up to one week's normal intake.
  • “Hire by week N” counts recruiting time. If the crew for your next delivery is more than one week's intake, the Operations screen now tells you to start hiring early enough to have them trained in time, instead of a week or two late.

Small airlines also no longer sit one person short of their requirement. See on-time performance for how staffing affects your schedule.

October 29, 2026

Real-world fares and flight costs (new games)

Alongside the new passenger demand, new games now use fares and flight costs checked against real data. Real US economy fares barely rise with distance: a short hop costs nearly as much as a medium-haul trip, and coast-to-coast is far cheaper per kilometre. The old fares rose steeply with distance, so short hops were half price and coast-to-coast about 30% too dear. Old flight costs had the same flaw: they had no take-off cost, so short hops were almost free to fly.

  • Domestic fares follow the real curve. In every country, short domestic hops now pay more and long domestic stages less: Boston–New York goes from $93 to $117, New York–Los Angeles from $381 to $301. International fares are unchanged.
  • Every flight pays for its take-off. Fuel and crew now include a fixed amount for taxi, take-off and climb on every departure, with a lower per-kilometre rate to match. Each aircraft costs exactly what it used to on its typical mission (about 1,200 km for a narrowbody, 6,000 km for a widebody), so short hops cost more and long stages a little less.
  • Gate to gate takes longer. Each flight now includes taxi and climb time on the block-hour clock, so an aircraft flies fewer short hops a week: about 44 Boston–New York round trips for an A320neo, down from 58. Schedules use the same times.

The result: short-haul is no longer the easy money it was, and long-haul international is unchanged. Long domestic routes in a single-class cabin are a bit harder, so they reward premium seats and the right-sized aircraft, much as they do for real airlines. Like the demand changes, this goes about two-thirds of the way to the real numbers. Games already in progress are unchanged. See the route economics guide.

October 29, 2026

Map view, reorganised from your feedback

The map view (the beta layout where the world map fills the screen) has a new layout, built from a player’s review of the first version:

  • Everything is on the bottom bar, one click each. Seven groups: Search, Network, Fleet, World, Operations, Service and Finance. A group opens straight onto a page, and the other pages in it sit as tabs along the top. Search opens the Route Finder, with the Route Planner one tab over. No page has two buttons any more.
  • Pages sorted where you’d look for them. The departure board and schedule live under Network. Crew, maintenance and fuel are under Operations, and marketing, catering, ancillaries, reputation and loyalty under Service. Finance splits into statements, loans and forecast, analysis and breakdown.
  • Cash, last week’s result and the date in one row at the top, in bigger type. A green or red figure next to your cash shows how much it went up or down last week.
  • Alerts down the right edge. Idle aircraft, expiring leases, loss-making routes and world events each get an icon. Hover for the details, or click to go straight there.
  • See an airport’s whole network. Click any airport code or pin on the map to light up every route at that airport.
  • A big airline logo top left, with Guide, Tutorial and Discord top right, and a Map / Dashboard switch bottom left.
  • Smoother panning and zooming on big networks: the map no longer blurs every route line and every button on each frame.

The classic layout is unchanged. You can switch between the two any time from Settings.

October 29, 2026

Map view runs smoothly again

The new map view (the beta layout where the world map fills the screen) could get very laggy as soon as you opened a page over the map. That’s fixed:

  • Pages opened over the map (Dashboard, Finance, Routes and the rest) scroll and respond at full speed again. In our tests they had been running at about half speed.
  • The map behind an open page now waits until you close it before it updates, instead of redrawing your whole network behind the page every time something changed.
  • Advancing the week on the map no longer redraws every route. Lines that move from profit to loss (or back) just change colour, and the numbers in the tooltips update in place.

The classic layout is unchanged. You can switch between the two any time from the settings menu.

October 29, 2026

Rival airlines now fly freight

Freight was the one business the AI airlines never touched: your freighters only ever competed with each other. Not any more. In new games, established full-service rivals start freight arms of their own and compete with you for the cargo.

  • Once a legacy or premium rival has a real passenger network and money to spare, it starts flying freighters on lanes from its hub. Most run a few lanes; airlines based at big freight hubs like Hong Kong, Frankfurt or Dubai run more. Budget carriers stay out of freight.
  • Rival freighters share a lane’s freight with yours on the same terms as two of your own freighters would: by how much each airline lifts, weighted by price. A rival charging under the market rate takes more than its share; one charging over takes less.
  • Rivals run their freight the way they run their passenger routes: they size each lane to what they can sell, add flights where their freighters fill, cut back where they fly light, and pull out of lanes that keep losing money. Copycat and aggressive carriers go after your freight lanes once your airline is big enough to notice.
  • Your freight routes now name every rival on the lane, with their weekly tonnage and rate, so a drop in tonnage is never a mystery. You also get a heads-up when a rival moves onto one of your freight lanes, and rival freight launches, cuts and new flights appear in the News tab.
  • The Competition tab lists each rival’s freight lanes: rate, frequency, capacity and aircraft, with the lanes you fly too marked as contested.
  • Buy a rival and its freight lanes come with it as your freight routes, flown by its freighters at the rates it was charging. Rivals that merge with each other keep their freight lanes too.
  • A rival in a custom set with a fleet preference only flies freighters from its own makers, or none.

It’s on by default for new games, and there’s a Rivals fly freight switch under Rivals on the setup screen if you’d rather keep freight to yourself. Games already in progress are unchanged. Also fixed: a rival flying freight out of a city’s second airport (Newark rather than JFK, say) is now counted against your freighters on the same lane. More on how rivals behave in the competition & alliances guide, and on choosing freighters in the freighter guide.

October 28, 2026

Fleet summary: your whole fleet, one row per aircraft type

The Fleet page has a new Summary view next to List, By Type and By Category. It’s a compact table with one row for each aircraft type you fly, showing:

  • how many you have and what share of the fleet that is
  • how many are owned and how many leased, plus how many more are on order
  • average age, and the age of the newest and oldest airframe
  • how many are idle, standing by as reserves, or down for maintenance
  • total seats, or tonnes for freighters
  • average utilisation, weekly lease and maintenance cost, and the book value of the aircraft you own

A Fleet total row sits at the bottom. Click any column to sort by it, and the table remembers your choice. Click a type to jump to the list showing just those aircraft. Types you’ve ordered but haven’t received yet get a row too, so you can see where the fleet is heading. Plan renewals with the aircraft guide.

Headwinds has it too.

October 28, 2026

Try the new Map view (beta), with a satellite map

There’s now a second way to lay out the game: the world map fills the screen and everything else floats over it. Your cash and the countdown to next week sit at the top, the main pages are round buttons down each side, and Company, Search, Network and Market run along the bottom. Every page opens in a panel over the map, and the buttons stay live, so you can hop between pages without closing anything.

It’s opt-in and nothing changes unless you turn it on: press Try it on the strip under the menus, or the globe button in the top bar (on a phone, ··· → Try map view). To go back, open ⚙ in the bottom-right corner and pick Back to classic layout. The choice is remembered on each device.

Map view also brings a satellite map made from NASA’s Blue Marble imagery. There’s a Satellite / Dark switch on the Network map too, so you can use either in either layout; the classic layout stays on the dark map unless you pick Satellite. The imagery softens once you zoom in past roughly country level. It’s a beta, so rough edges and feedback are both expected — the Discord is the place for it.

Headwinds is getting it too.

October 27, 2026

The Gates list remembers how you sorted it

Airports → Your Gates now keeps the column and direction you last sorted by, and whether you picked Table or Cards. Leave the tab, advance the week or reload, and it comes back the way you left it instead of falling back to region order. Until you sort, the list starts in the usual order.

Suggested by VodkaOnFire on Discord. Added to Headwinds as well.

October 27, 2026

Keep marketing at a share of revenue

Brand Marketing (Operations) has a new % of revenue option next to the usual fixed weekly budget. Pick a share, from 0.5% to 8% or anything up to 25%, and each week your brand spend is set to that share of that week’s revenue. It grows as the airline grows and eases off in a bad week, so you no longer have to keep raising the figure by hand. Your P&L shows exactly the share you chose, and awareness builds from what you actually spend. Per-airport targeted campaigns stay as fixed amounts on top. Switching to % of revenue starts from the share you’re spending today, and switching back keeps last week’s spend as your fixed budget.

Suggested by Barca on Discord. Added to Headwinds as well.

October 26, 2026

Your logo on the fuselage

Liveries have a new Logo on the fuselage option, next to Logo on the tail. Tick it and your logo is painted on the front of the fuselage, just ahead of your airline’s name, the way most real airlines wear it. The name moves back to make room. Use it with or without the tail logo, and with or without the name. It’s off for every livery you’ve already saved, so nothing changes until you turn it on in ✎ Edit Branding → Livery.

Suggested by Xen on Discord. Added to Headwinds as well.

October 22, 2026

Schedule your week

  • A Schedule tab under Operations. Every aircraft gets a row with its week laid out from Monday to Sunday, each flight drawn as a round trip. Drag a flight to choose when it leaves, or drag one in from the aircraft’s list of routes. Anything you don’t place is scheduled for you, so the whole thing is optional: open it when you want to tidy a timetable, ignore it when you don’t. Times show in your hub’s local time or in UTC, and you can zoom in to 2× or 4×. With a flight selected, the arrow keys move it by 15 minutes (an hour with Shift).
  • The departure board follows your schedule. Your flights now leave at the times you set, shown in each airport’s local time.
  • Charters are on it too. A charter shows as a fixed, striped block on the aircraft flying it. You can see how much of the week it takes, and your own flights are scheduled around it, but the customer decides when it flies, so it can’t be moved.
  • The schedule is for planning and for the board. It doesn’t change demand or costs, and an aircraft can still fly only as many hours a week as before (see the fleet planning guide).

October 22, 2026

Fewer clicks: shortcuts, flights from the Fleet page, and your families in the Market

  • A shortcuts bar. Every page in the Network, Fleet, Airports and Company menus now has a ☆ beside it. Star up to eight and they appear as buttons on a bar under the menus, one click away. Click the ★ again, or the × on a shortcut, to remove it. Shortcuts are kept in your browser, so they stay put across saves and new games.
  • Change flights from the Fleet page. Every route on an aircraft's card now has its own −/+ for flights per week, and Adjust flights on all routes sets every route the plane flies to the same number in one go — or adds or removes flights on each, or fills the aircraft's spare hours. Tick several aircraft in the fleet table and Flights/wk on the selection bar does the same for all of their routes. Freighters included. The usual limits apply: no route goes past the aircraft's flying hours or the gate slots, and you are told what stopped it.
  • “Your families” in the Market. A new Show only chip lists just the aircraft families you already fly or have on order — your types plus their stretches, shrinks and freighter versions, which share your crews and your maintenance set-up — so ordering more of what you fly no longer means scrolling the whole catalogue. Every type is in the aircraft guide.

All three suggested by VodkaOnFire on Discord.

October 22, 2026

Route Finder: how much of a market is already flown

  • A Served column. Beside each market's size, the Route Finder now shows how much of it is already being flown, as a percentage. It counts rivals' nonstops, their one-stop connections over their hubs, and your own flights. Low means there is room for you; close to 100% means a new route would mostly win passengers from someone else. Hover over the figure to see who carries what, and how many travellers a week nobody carries yet. It comes from the same market-share calculation as your weekly results, for a fully established route this month.
  • Sort by “Most demand left”. Ranks markets by the travellers nobody carries yet, so a huge lane rivals already fill drops below a smaller one nobody flies.
  • The freight finder catches up. Its freighter list now starts with your own freighters, with how many you have, how many are idle and the range of your best one. A new Show lanes I already serve switch brings back the lanes you fly, labelled with your route. It also gets the Served column, counting your own freighters, and the Most demand left sort. Plan → now takes the freighter you were searching with to the planner.
  • The freight planner lists your freighters first, with how many are idle, and picks one of yours for the forecast instead of the first freighter in the catalogue.
  • The From box starts with your network. In both finders it now opens on the airports you picked recently, then your hubs and focus cities, then the other airports where you hold gates. Typing still searches every airport, with your own listed first. The other airport drop-downs in the game also gain a Recently Used group, and list the regions you fly in first.

Thanks to VodkaOnFire on Discord for all of these.

October 21, 2026

A faster Route Finder

Sorting the Route Finder by profit could take several seconds on a big airline, every time you opened it or changed the search. Each row's forecast plays out a full week of your network with that route added, so it can count connecting passengers, and a profit sort needs 150 of them. Three changes, prompted by VodkaOnFire on Discord:

  • It opens on your last forecasts. The finder now remembers the figures it worked out, per airline and aircraft, even after a reload or a new week. When you come back, the table is ranked straight away. The old figures are dimmed, with the week they're from in the tooltip, and fresh ones replace them in the background. Plan → always forecasts the route from scratch, so an older figure can't change the route you actually open.
  • Switching aircraft is about 6× faster. The network-week part of a forecast doesn't depend on the aircraft, but it was being redone for every row. It is now reused when you switch aircraft on the same lanes.
  • Forecasting runs in the background, on spare processor cores. The page stays responsive while the numbers come in. On a 4-core machine, a 150-row profit sort took about 1.6 seconds instead of 4.2. The numbers are exactly the same as before.

October 21, 2026

Lease gates from the map

  • Tap an airport, lease a gate. An airport's page now opens with a Lease a Gate card: what the next gate costs each month, what it adds to your weekly bill, and a button to lease it. Tap any airport on the network map and it is right there, so you can find somewhere new on the map and open a gate without a trip to the Airports tab.
  • Your own airports open too. Before, only the dim background airports on the map could be tapped. Your hubs and the airports you already fly to now open the same page, so adding a gate where you are short of slots takes a couple of taps.
  • Airport pages fit a phone. On a narrow screen the page now shows one card per row. Before, half the cards, the lounge among them, sat off the right-hand edge.

Thanks to Alex585975 for the idea on Discord. New to gates? The how-to-play guide covers what they do.

October 21, 2026

Rival sets: more than one maker, and fixes

  • Several manufacturers per airline. A rival in a custom set can now name more than one aircraft maker, as a list like "maker": ["Boeing", "Embraer"] or as "Boeing, Embraer". It buys from any of them, picking the best-sized aircraft for each route. A misspelt maker is skipped with a warning and the rest still count. The competition guide now lists every maker name the game knows, with the years each one's aircraft were built.
  • Historical airlines arrive on time. In era games, the game's own random start-ups could fill the field and leave a set's later airlines waiting for years, or never appearing at all. Start-ups no longer take the room a set airline is waiting for, so every airline in your set joins in its founding year.
  • Fleet preferences hold as airlines grow. A rival that filled its biggest preferred aircraft used to step up to another maker's (an all-Boeing carrier buying A380s). It now stays on what it prefers. Routes it could only open with another maker's aircraft can still grow.
  • Copying a field keeps founding years. Copying your rivals from the Competition screen gave airlines that joined mid-game your start year, so a shared copy brought them in early. Each now keeps the year it was founded.

More in the competition guide.

October 18, 2026

Reserves by airport

Pick the Reserve filter on the Fleet page and a new Reserves by base panel shows where your standby aircraft are parked: each airport, how many reserves it holds, and how many of each type. Click an airport to list only its reserves, or click a type to narrow it to, say, just the A320s at that base.

October 18, 2026

More control over your rivals

  • Fix: custom rival sets now work. Games started from a pasted set were quietly getting the random field instead. If you started one, start it again.
  • Fleet preference. A rival in a set can list the aircraft it flies, or just a manufacturer: an all-Boeing carrier stays all-Boeing as it grows, and with production lines it competes for slots on those lines. When nothing it prefers can fly a route, it takes whatever fits.
  • Closing years. In era games, a rival can now close in a given year as well as open in one, so a set of historical airlines rises and falls on schedule. An airline that has already closed by your start year never appears.
  • Starting routes and a second hub. A set can give a rival its real starting network and a second hub, instead of a generated one. Any listed route no aircraft of the era can fly is left out, and the game tells you which.
  • Random logos. Give any rival in a set the logo "random", or shuffle every logo at once with "randomLogos": true. Random logos are spread evenly, so a big set doesn't repeat one over and over.
  • A chance to appear. A rival in a set can have a chance from 0 to 100, so a long list of airlines gives a different field every game. It leans toward underserved markets: an airline is likelier to appear where few others are based near its hub. Thanks to VodkaOnFire for both ideas.
  • How many rivals. Start with a few (10), the usual 25, or many (40).
  • Rival pressure. Relaxed rivals pay you less attention, start fewer fare wars and move less often; fierce ones watch you from early on and move more often.
  • New airlines and mergers. Random start-ups can now be none, rare, normal or frequent, and you can stop rivals merging with each other.

All on the setup screen under Rivals, for new games. More in the competition guide.

October 17, 2026

Choose your rivals

New games have a Rivals section on the setup screen, so you decide who you’re up against.

  • Custom rival sets. Paste in a set of airlines, each with a name, home airport, tier and size (small, medium or large). Optionally add a founding year, logo, personality and quality. Play with only your set, or add it to the usual random field. A set can start with up to 60 rivals.
  • Rivals founded in their own year. In era games, an airline founded after your start year appears once the calendar reaches its year, if there’s room in the field.
  • Share a field. The Competition tab copies any game’s rivals as a set you can post or paste into a new game. The airlines still to be founded come with it.
  • No rival at your hub. Start without any rival based at your home airport. Others still fly in.
  • No random new airlines. Switch off the random start-ups that appear mid-game, so a custom set plays exactly as written.

More in the competition guide.

October 17, 2026

Production lines: you and your rivals share the factory

Until now every airline had its own private delivery queue, and rival airlines didn’t queue at all: when one decided to grow, its new aircraft appeared that week. In new games, aircraft now come off production lines that you share with the rivals, and they have to order and wait just like you.

  • One line per aircraft family. Each family (737NG, A320neo, 777 and so on) has one factory line building a set number of aircraft a week: more for turboprops, fewer for jumbos. When rivals book the weeks you wanted, you wait longer, or you pick a type on a quieter line.
  • Rivals order and wait too. A rival opening a route, adding flights or moving to a bigger type now orders the aircraft first. The change happens when they arrive, so you can see it coming in the news. Rivals with plenty of cash will pay for early slots when a line is busy, and they move to another type when their favourite is booked solid.
  • Pay to jump the queue. The order form shows the line’s next weeks. The standard week is list price; earlier weeks cost up to 25% more. Your own deliveries from one line arrive at least a set gap apart, from a week for turboprops to five weeks for jumbos.
  • See who is buying. Every aircraft in the market shows how many are flying and on order across the game, which airlines hold them, and how busy its line is. This works in every game, old saves included.
  • Purchases are paid in stages. A deposit when you sign, instalments as delivery approaches, and the remaining three quarters on the week the aircraft arrives. The order form warns you if the balance would take your cash negative.
  • Era games: launch customers. New types are announced two years before they enter service. For six months after the announcement you can sign up as a launch customer: at least 20 to 30 aircraft, paid in full, at a discount that grows each time you launch another type from the same manufacturer, with the first slots on the line. Launch orders are firm and cannot be cancelled.

Production lines are on by default for new games and can be switched off on the setup screen. Games already running keep their private queues. More in the fleet planning guide.

October 17, 2026

Lighter cabins now add range sooner

  • The real ultra-long 787-9 routes now work. Qantas flies Perth–London (14,508 km) and Melbourne–Dallas with a 236-seat 787-9, and Air New Zealand flies Auckland–New York with about 275 seats. In the game none of these reached, because taking seats out of a cabin added range too slowly.
  • How it works now. At the typical cabin an aircraft is at its take-off weight with the tanks a few percent short of full. Each passenger you leave off becomes fuel at the same rate that packing in an extra one costs it, until the tanks are full, up to 5% more range. A 787-9 with 236 seats now reaches about 14,850 km, against 14,140 km at its typical 290.
  • The maximum hasn’t changed. A light cabin still adds at most 5%. You just reach it after removing a few dozen seats rather than every seat. Packed cabins lose range exactly as before, and nothing that flew before is affected. Added to Headwinds as well.

October 17, 2026

Fix: long routes near an aircraft’s range wouldn’t open

  • The Route Planner counted your cabin twice. Since range started depending on seats, the planner took an aircraft’s range with its cabin already counted, then counted the cabin’s weight again for the forecast. A route your aircraft could reach, but only with a few hundred kilometres to spare, showed no forecast and no Open Route button. For example, an A340-300 with 362 seats reaches 12,351 km, but the planner treated it as about 11,300 km and wouldn’t open LA–Sydney (12,061 km). The planner, the cargo planner and the “Best aircraft for this route” table now use the range your aircraft really has.

October 17, 2026

Runway length now counts when you move routes

Moving a route to another aircraft no longer lets you put it on a plane that cannot use the runway. Thanks to Barca for the report on Discord.

  • Routes → move to another aircraft and Fleet → Transfer Routes now check the runway at every airport the route touches, including stops on a multi-stop route.
  • An aircraft that needs more runway than an airport has is greyed out at the bottom of the list, with the reason: for example “Runway too short at SNA: the A321neo needs 5,950 ft, SNA has 5,700 ft”.
  • Routes that were already flying into a short runway before the rule existed keep working, and can still move to an aircraft that needs no more runway than the one flying it today.

October 17, 2026

Release year on the aircraft market

Every aircraft in Fleet → Market now shows the year it entered service, so you can tell a fresh design from an old one at a glance. Thanks to VodkaOnFire for the suggestion on Discord.

  • Cards show “Introduced 1998” next to the manufacturer.
  • Table view has a new Year column you can sort by, newest or oldest first.
  • Era games: under the year, the table tells you when passengers start marking the design down. It turns yellow five years out and red once the design has dated, with the quality points it is costing you.
  • Fix: the “Dates from” badge on market cards was one year early. It now names the first year passengers actually mark the design down.

October 17, 2026

Design your own livery

Open ✎ Edit Branding → Livery and paint your airline: fuselage, tail and winglets, engines, a cheatline, swoosh, belly, retro or tail-wrap style, your name on the fuselage and your logo on the fin. It is painted onto a real Boeing 737-800 illustration and shows on your Fleet page.

  • Every airline already has a livery in its logo colour — the editor is there when you want to make it yours. “Surprise me” rolls a random scheme if you would rather not design one.
  • One aircraft type for now. Each extra type (787, A380, ATR…) costs $15 in artwork licensing; a $15 donation adds the type you fly for everyone.
  • Also live in Headwinds, where your planes on the globe fly in your colours too.

October 17, 2026

Range corrections for 22 aircraft

With range now tied to a typical cabin, we checked every aircraft’s range against its maker’s figure at that cabin. 22 types were wrong: most too generous, a few too short. Added to Headwinds as well.

  • The biggest correction is the 747SP, from 15,400 km to 10,800 km at 276 seats.
  • Others that lost range: the Tu-154M (4,250 km), DC-9-50 (2,408 km), 737 MAX 8-200 (5,000 km), 737-500 (4,398 km), 720B (5,926 km), DC-8-30 (7,417 km), MC-21-300 (6,000 km), Beechcraft 1900D (1,259 km with all 19 seats filled), Cessna Grand Caravan EX (1,689 km), Short 360 (1,056 km), Viscount 700 and 800 (2,140 and 2,220 km), MA600 (1,430 km) and Il-14 (1,305 km).
  • Aircraft that gained range: the Trident 3B (3,593 km), 737-200 (4,815 km), Superjet 100 (3,530 km) and Pilatus PC-12 (3,339 km, quoted with four passengers aboard, as Pilatus does).
  • The A350-900 now uses Airbus’s current figure: 15,400 km at its typical cabin, up from 15,000 km. Packed to 440 seats it reaches about 13,600 km.
  • The 737 family is now quoted on one basis, so the -700 (5,575 km), -800 (5,436 km) and -900ER (5,463 km) compare fairly with each other.
  • Your existing routes are untouched. A route you were flying before the range update keeps the aircraft’s old figure. Routes you open from now on use the corrected one. If you opened a route on one of these aircraft since then and it’s now out of range, the out-of-range notice flags it and says when a lighter cabin would fix it.
  • Some figures we left alone. A few aircraft that looked off, such as the Super Constellation and the Islander, turned out to be quoted on a different but valid basis, so they keep their current range.

The narrow-body and turboprop guides list the corrected ranges, and the wide-body guide has the new A350-900 figure.

October 17, 2026

Range now depends on how many seats you fit

Aircraft makers quote range with a typical cabin: 525 seats on an A380, 396 on a 777-300ER, 165 on an A320neo. Until now the game gave every aircraft that range even when packed to its exit limit, which no real aircraft can do. Every aircraft now has its maker’s typical seat count, and range follows the cabin you fit. Added to Headwinds as well.

  • At the typical seat count you get the full quoted range. The marketplace now shows which cabin that is, for example “15,200 km at 525 seats”. Hover over it to see the range with every seat filled.
  • Packing in more seats costs range. Every passenger past the typical number, about 100 kg with bags, is fuel the aircraft can’t carry. An A380 packed to 853 seats reaches about 12,900 km, and a 777-300ER packed to 550 about 11,600 km. On short and medium routes this costs you nothing, so packing a cabin is still a good way to earn more on them.
  • Fewer seats than typical adds little. At the typical cabin the tanks are already nearly full, so stripping seats out adds 5% at most.
  • New aircraft arrive with the typical cabin. The order screen starts at the typical seat count and shows the range as you change the cabin. The Route Planner has an “all economy, typical seats” default and a separate “packed to the limit” option.
  • The ultra-long-range A350s are now quoted at 18,000 km with Singapore’s 161-seat cabin and Qantas’ 238-seat cabin. Packed full, neither can reach Sydney–London.
  • Your existing routes are untouched. Every route you were flying when this update arrived keeps the old rule on the aircraft flying it. A route you open from now on, or an existing route you move to another aircraft, uses the new rule. If a new route is out of range and a lighter cabin would fix it, the out-of-range notice tells you which cabin.
  • AI rivals follow the same rule. On routes they open from now on, they carry as many seats as the distance allows: every seat on short and medium routes, fewer close to the aircraft’s range. Their existing routes keep the capacity they have.

Planning long-haul? The wide-body guide now lists each aircraft’s range at its typical cabin and fully packed, and fleet planning covers matching aircraft to missions.

October 17, 2026

Crew: staying fully staffed in long games

  • “Replace leavers automatically” now hires ahead. It used to rehire someone only after they had left, and the replacement then needed recruiting and training time. That meant every group ran a few people short forever, even at top pay, with an on-time penalty and a “Short-handed” warning that never went away. Now it also keeps the people expected to leave during training already in the pipeline, so your crews sit at full strength. It still only replaces leavers: crew for new aircraft is still your hire.
  • Reserve crews cover tiny gaps. Every group’s requirement already includes standby and reserve crews. A gap of 1% or less is now flown by those reserves, with no on-time penalty and no warning. The crew card shows it as “short, covered by reserves”. A small airline missing one person out of twenty is still short.
  • Top pay is worth paying for. Resignations used to stop falling at about 1.9× pay, so the last stretch of the pay slider cost more and changed nothing. They now keep falling all the way to 2.0×. The lowest rate, about 3% a year from retirements and moves, hasn’t changed, and nothing changes below market pay.

October 17, 2026

New aircraft: the Airbus A350-1000ULR

One of the most requested aircraft on the Discord, added to Headwinds as well.

  • What it is. The A350 Qantas ordered for Project Sunrise: an A350-1000 with an extra 20,000-litre fuel tank and a higher take-off weight, built to fly Sydney to London and Sydney to New York nonstop. The photo is the real first aircraft, test-flying out of Melbourne in its Project Sunrise colours.
  • How it plays. With every seat filled (480) it reaches about 14,600 km: the aircraft hits its weight limit before the extra tank can be filled. Every seat you take out becomes fuel, so a light cabin is where the range comes from. A Qantas-style 238-seat cabin reaches 18,000 km, enough for Sydney–London, and a lighter one up to about 18,900 km. It also costs more to buy and lease, and burns about 4% more fuel than a standard -1000, so it only pays on routes that genuinely need the range.
  • The A350-900ULR now works the same way. It used to fly 440 passengers 18,000 km, which the real aircraft can’t do: Singapore Airlines flies it with 161 seats and no economy cabin. Packed full it now reaches about 13,700 km, and a Singapore-style 161-seat cabin takes it to 18,000 km. A Singapore-style cabin still reaches Singapore–New York. If you fly one far with a dense cabin, the route will show as out of range, and the notice will tell you which lighter cabin brings it back.
  • Range on screen. The marketplace shows each aircraft’s range at the cabin it is quoted with, for example “18,000 km at 238 seats”. An aircraft’s own page in your fleet now shows its real range with its current cabin and any engine or wingtip options, instead of the catalogue figure.
  • When you can get one. In classic games it’s in the marketplace now. In era games it enters service in 2027, the same year Qantas takes its first one.

Planning ultra-long-haul? The wide-body guide lines it up against the A350-900ULR and the 777X-8, and route economics covers when the longest routes pay.

October 17, 2026

Route Finder keeps its ranking when you lease a gate

  • No more reset after + Gate. Leasing a gate from a Route Finder row used to throw away every forecast, so a list sorted by best profit fell back to biggest market and started forecasting all 150 markets again. The finder now keeps showing the previous figures, dimmed, while it updates them, and the list stays in profit order and re-ranks itself as the new numbers come in.
  • Forecasts survive a trip to the planner. Going to Plan → and coming back no longer starts the forecasting from scratch either.

October 16, 2026

Faster screens, route hours and runways, and bulk frequency changes

  • Less lag on big airlines. The Routes and Gates screens and the Route Finder now do their work in far fewer passes, and stop recalculating everything when you click something unrelated. The Route Finder shows forecasts as they are worked out instead of freezing until the whole list is done.
  • Hours and Runway on the Routes page. Two new sortable columns: Hours is the block time of one flight (hover for the weekly flying it takes), and Runway is the shorter of the two runways at either end, which is the one that decides what can fly the route. The routes table now shows 25 rows at a time, with a button for more.
  • Bulk frequency. Like bulk pricing, but for flights a week. Change the frequency on many routes in one go, from the Routes header (filtered by how full the routes are) or from a selection of routes. Each route moves as far as its aircraft’s flying hours and the gate slots allow, and the preview tells you which limit stopped it. Fill spare hours shares an aircraft’s spare hours across its routes instead of handing them all to the first one.
  • Gates. Your gate list shows 25 airports at a time, and browsing a region lists the top few airports in each country with a button for the rest.

More on choosing frequencies in the route economics guide.

October 16, 2026

Replace ageing aircraft automatically

Re-equipping the same routes with newer aircraft used to mean ordering, waiting for delivery, moving every route by hand, then selling or returning the old aircraft, one at a time. Now an order can say which aircraft it replaces, and the swap happens by itself on delivery.

  • Replace on delivery. When you order, pick which of your aircraft each new one replaces. You can also set or change this later from any order in your order queue. When the new aircraft arrives it takes over every route of the old one, with the same frequencies and fares and no relaunch cost, and the routes keep their maturity.
  • Bulk replace. Select aircraft on the Fleet page and choose Replace. You get a list of types that can take over their routes, showing how many of your selection each one fits and the change in seats. Pick one and the order form opens with the replacements already filled in, oldest aircraft first.
  • Choose what happens to the old aircraft. Sell it (owned) or hand it back to the lessor (leased, on the normal early-return terms), or keep it as a spare. The order form estimates the early-return fee before you commit, and warns you if a lease will run out before its replacement arrives.
  • It still has to fit. A replacement has to be able to fly the old aircraft’s routes: range, runways, airport rules and weekly flying hours are all checked, and aircraft that don’t fit are greyed out with the reason. If the old aircraft is in the shop or flying a charter when the new one arrives, the new one waits and takes over as soon as it’s free.

Opening new routes is still up to you. This only takes the repetition out of renewing the ones you already fly. More on picking replacements in fleet planning.

October 16, 2026

World events are fairer to established airlines

Players reported that recessions, pandemic scares and other world events made the game very hard from around year three. They were right. A small airline barely feels a downturn, because even a weakened market still fills its few flights. Once your network is sized to its markets, every downturn hits in full, and a couple of rules made that much worse than intended.

  • Overlapping events can no longer halve your demand. No single world event moves demand by more than 30%, but two of them used to stack (a recession on top of a pandemic scare, say), which could cut a route's market roughly in half for months. The 30% limit now applies to the combined effect on each route.
  • One downturn at a time. A global downturn (recession, pandemic scare or industry fare war) no longer starts while another downturn is already running. Separate regional slumps in different parts of the world can still overlap.
  • The AI airlines feel it too. Rival carriers used to sail through recessions, pandemic scares and fuel spikes untouched. Now their loads and profits suffer exactly like yours, and the weaker ones trim service, so a downturn can be a chance to take ground.
  • Strikes stay at the struck airport. A Heathrow ground-staff strike now hits routes through Heathrow only, not every route in the UK.
  • The AI notices you gradually. Rivals used to switch from ignoring you to targeting you the moment your airline passed $100M in value. That attention now builds steadily with your size, and fare wars become more likely as you grow rather than all switching on at once.

More on how rivals behave in competition and alliances, and on protecting yourself from fuel spikes in fuel hedging.

October 16, 2026

Six more airports in Egypt

Another batch requested on the Discord, added to Headwinds as well.

  • Sphinx (SPX) in Giza has low-cost and Gulf flying. Capital International (CCE) in the New Administrative Capital, east of Cairo, only started scheduled flights this year. Both are part of Greater Cairo, so they share its market with Cairo International, the way London’s airports share London’s, so flying from them competes for the same passengers instead of creating new ones.
  • Sohag (HMB) serves the Nile valley between Asyut and Luxor, and most of its traffic goes to Saudi Arabia and the Gulf.
  • Abu Simbel (ABS) sits beside the temples near the Sudanese border. Nearly everyone who flies there is a tourist coming from Cairo or Aswan.
  • El Alamein (DBB) and Marsa Matruh (MUH) serve Egypt’s Mediterranean coast, a summer beach destination for Cairo, the Gulf and charter flights from Europe.

Thinking about a second base in a city you already serve? Hub strategy covers when a second airport is worth it, and route economics covers what makes a new route pay.

October 16, 2026

Every airport on the map, and a route finder that fits a phone

  • The whole world on the network map. Every airport in the game now shows as a small grey dot under your own network, so you can see where places actually are before you fly there. The big airports show at every zoom; the smaller regional fields fill in as you zoom toward them, and their codes appear once there is room to read them.
  • Hover for a name, click for the details. Hovering a dot gives the airport's name, city and size. Clicking it (or tapping it on a phone) opens the same airport page you get anywhere else in the game.
  • A map from day one. A brand-new airline with no routes used to get an empty "no routes yet" box. Now it gets the map, centred on your hub, which makes it a good place to look for your first destinations.
  • Too busy? The All airports switch in the map's legend hides the dots, and the game remembers your choice.
  • Route finder on phones. On a narrow screen each destination now leads with its airport code, puts the city underneath in small type and shortens the badges (+2 instead of +2 airports). Distance, demand and the forecast now fit on screen next to it instead of sitting off the edge. The passenger and freight finders both get this. Desktop is unchanged.

New to picking routes? The route economics guide covers what makes a market worth flying.

October 16, 2026

Smaller touches: typeable counts and better photos

  • Type a number instead of clicking. Departures and other counts now use the same minus / box / plus control as seat allocation, so you can type the number you want.
  • Better aircraft photos for the Tu-104, C-47, SSJ100, E195, A320ceo, 737-500 and 777X-8.

October 15, 2026

Cloud saves for supporters

Your airline can now follow you between browsers and devices.

  • Three cloud slots. Open Save / Load and sign in with your Headwinds account (Google, Discord or an email link). Supporters can upload an airline to a cloud slot on one device and load it on any other.
  • A thank-you, not a purchase. Uploading is switched on for people who support the game. If you stop, the cloud saves you already have stay yours to load. Nothing in the game itself changes, for anyone.
  • Two devices, no surprises. If a cloud slot changed on another device since you last looked, the game shows you what is there now and asks before replacing it.
  • New device? The new-game screen has a Load from a save slot or the cloud link, so you can pick up an airline without founding a new one first.

Cloud saves are best effort, on the same hobby servers as Headwinds. Saving in your browser works exactly as before. Step by step, including phones, in the FAQ.

October 14, 2026

New game option: randomized passenger demand

An idea from VodkaOnFire on the Discord: what if the map you know weren’t the answer?

  • Realistic or Randomized. The Launch step has a new Passenger demand choice. Realistic is the game as it has always been. Randomized rolls every airport’s passenger traffic before you start.
  • Bigger swings at smaller airports. Mega airports roll between −20% and +10%, majors between −30% and +50%, and regional airports between −50% and +100%. A city with several airports rolls once for all of them, so London is one roll, not five.
  • Tiers follow the dice. A major airport that booms far enough becomes a mega, and a mega that slumps far enough drops to major. The same happens between major and regional. A tier change moves the airport’s gate and landing fees, and changes which airports rival airlines target and how big a rival based there grows. By default a major can only become a mega when a mega has dropped out, so the world never has more megas than the real one. Tick Allow more mega airports to lift that cap.
  • The world stays the same size. After the rolls, the world’s total passenger market is brought back to its real-world level, so demand moves between cities rather than appearing from nowhere. Rival airlines play in the same world you do.
  • Shareable worlds. Every randomized world has a number. Give a friend the number and the same mega setting and they get the same world. Your hub’s roll is only revealed when you launch, and each airport’s page shows its roll and whether it changed tier.

New to picking a base? Hub strategy and route economics still apply. You just can’t take the numbers for granted.

October 13, 2026

Sort every airport in the game, and filter the aircraft market

Two requests from VodkaOnFire on the Discord.

  • All airports table. The Airports tab has a new All airports view next to By region. It lists all 2,134 airports in pages of 50, and you can sort any column: passenger market, cargo market, metro population, longest runway, how many airlines fly there, your gates and the cost of the next gate. Filter by name, region or tier, then jump straight to an airport’s details or add a gate.
  • Passenger and cargo market. These two columns add up every city pair from an airport — the same demand the Route Planner and Cargo Planner show you, totalled for the whole airport. Airports in the same city share that city’s market, so every New York airport shows New York’s. The passenger figure grows with your game’s calendar, so a 1960 world shows 1960-sized markets.
  • Aircraft market filters. Fleet → Market has a new Show only row. In production hides types you can only buy second-hand, Leasable now hides anything no lessor will lease you yet, and in era games Hide dated designs hides types passengers already mark down for age. The market remembers your choices, which helps once you are twenty years into a save.

Weighing up a type? The aircraft guide has every model’s numbers, and hub strategy covers picking where to grow.

October 13, 2026

Four more airports: Niigata, Noida, Leeds Bradford and Doncaster Sheffield

Another batch requested on the Discord, added to Headwinds as well.

  • Niigata (KIJ) serves Japan’s Sea of Japan coast, with domestic flying to Sapporo, Osaka and Fukuoka and short international hops to Seoul and Taipei.
  • Noida International (DXN) is Delhi’s new second airport at Jewar, which opened to airlines in June 2026. It shares Delhi’s market with Indira Gandhi International, the way London’s airports share London. It’s a long way out of town, so travellers favour it most for domestic trips. Long-haul passengers still lean heavily towards DEL.
  • Leeds Bradford (LBA) gives West Yorkshire its own airport for holiday and short-haul European flying.
  • Doncaster Sheffield (DSA) has had no airline flights since it closed in late 2022. It has a long runway, so it’s an open market for anyone who wants to bring South Yorkshire back on the map. It sits too close by road to Leeds Bradford and Humberside for flights between them to sell.

Choosing where to grow next? Hub strategy covers when a second airport in a city is worth it, and route economics covers what makes a new route pay.

October 9, 2026

Staff pay and hiring rework, plus gate slots in the Route Finder

Three requests from the Discord: Barca, Dunno23 and VodkaOnFire. All three are in Headwinds too.

  • Unions no longer table pay demands. Pay is now entirely your call. A demand used to count as refused if you didn’t answer it in time, and over a long game the demands pushed pay up toward the 2.0× ceiling. Any demand open in your save is withdrawn with no penalty. Strikes still happen when pay is low enough that morale falls below 50.
  • Hold a pay rate. Each staff group on the Labor screen now has a Hold this rate lock. A held group stays at the multiplier you set and pays the full premium every week. A group you don’t hold still drifts back toward market by about 6% a year, as before.
  • Recruiting depends on pay. In games where you hire your own crew, you can only take on so many recruits a week. A large hire is paid for up front. Recruits fill a queue week by week and then train as normal. The better you pay, the faster the queue fills. You can cancel the part of the queue not yet recruited and get that money back.
  • Lease gates from the Route Finder. Every passenger and freight result now shows how many weekly slots you have free at that airport. Your origin gets the same line above the list. Wherever you are short of a 7-flights-a-week route, there is a + Gate button, so you no longer have to open the planner to find out you have no gate.

October 8, 2026

Five new airports: London Southend and four in southern Italy

Another request from the Discord. All five are in now (in Headwinds too).

  • London Southend (SEN): London’s sixth airport, sharing the London market with Heathrow, Gatwick, Stansted, Luton and City. It draws a smaller slice of London demand than the big fields, but its 1,856 m runway takes an A320 or 737 comfortably.
  • Salerno Costa d’Amalfi (QSR): reopened to airlines in 2024 after its runway was extended, and the closest airport to the Amalfi Coast, so it gets a tourism boost. Salerno–Naples is a short train ride, so no flights between them.
  • Crotone (CRV) on Calabria’s Ionian coast, and Foggia Gino Lisa (FOG), the gateway to the Gargano. At 1,795 m, Foggia’s runway is the shortest of the five, so check your aircraft’s field requirements first.
  • Taranto-Grottaglie (TAR): a 3,200 m runway with no airline service at all in real life. It’s an open market for whoever wants to be first in. Taranto–Brindisi counts as a road trip, so no flights between them.

October 8, 2026

Jumbo jets, Concorde and freighters arrive on the right schedule

  • 747s and the A380 no longer arrive faster than a widebody. Every 747 passenger model and the A380 was being built on a regional jet’s schedule: about a month for the first one, then one every two weeks. They now take the longest of any airliner: 10 weeks for your first, then one every 5 weeks. Orders you’ve already placed keep their dates. Thanks to VodkaOnFire on Discord for spotting it.
  • Concorde and freighters fixed too. They had the same problem. Concorde now delivers on a widebody’s schedule. Freighters now go by size: an ATR 72F arrives like a turboprop, a 777F like a widebody, and the An-225 is as slow as a jumbo. Compare types on the aircraft guide.
  • The marketplace shows the real delivery date. The “Delivery in” figure on aircraft cards and in the comparison table left out the longer wait for the first aircraft of a type, so it often showed half the real time. It now matches the order form and when the aircraft actually arrives. Progress bars on pending orders now fill steadily from the day you order, too.
  • The Fleet screen’s category view now shows every aircraft. Jumbos, Concorde and freighters were missing from it. They now get their own sections.

October 3, 2026

Reset many routes to reference fares at once

  • New: Reset to ref on the bulk-edit bar. Tick several routes on the Routes screen and the bar that appears now has a Reset to ref button next to Apply %. It puts every cabin on the selected routes back to its market reference fare in one go, the same as the button in each route’s fare editor. You’re asked to confirm first, since it replaces any custom fares on those routes. See route economics for how reference fares work.
